stories.title: A healthier lifestyle went with less fatigue over 5 years
stories.summary: A study followed 839 people with MS for five years. Those who scored higher on activity, diet quality, meditation, not smoking and vitamin D had less fatigue, depression and disability.
stories.why: It shows a link, not proof that one causes the other. But it's a good reason to track your own habits.

stories.title: Light activity was tied to lower fatigue
stories.summary: In people newly diagnosed with MS, light physical activity (like easy walking) was the measure most strongly linked to lower fatigue, even after accounting for disability.
stories.why: You don't have to start with hard exercise. Gentle movement may help with fatigue.

stories.title: A Mediterranean-style diet eased fatigue in a small trial
stories.summary: A two-month trial with 90 people with MS compared diets. A modified Mediterranean diet (vegetables, whole grains, fish, olive oil) went with less fatigue.
stories.why: Small and early, but it points the same way as general healthy eating.

stories.title: A new MS pill cut relapses in two large trials
stories.summary: Novartis says its pill remibrutinib (a BTK inhibitor) reduced relapses more than teriflunomide in two Phase III trials of relapsing MS. Full results come at a conference this month.
stories.why: This is company news, and the full data isn't out yet. Something to ask your neurologist about later.

stories.title: BTK drugs: fewer relapses, but repair isn't proven yet
stories.summary: A review pooling trials found BTK inhibitors cut relapses and new MRI lesions. Disability didn't change in the short trials, and the hope that they help repair myelin comes only from lab and animal work so far.

stories.title: Some MS drugs may work partly by calming the immune response to a common virus
stories.summary: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is strongly linked to MS. A new study suggests anti-CD20 treatments may work partly by lowering the immune system's reaction to EBV.

stories.title: The year's biggest MS conference is next week
stories.summary: MSToronto2026, the joint meeting of the American and European MS research groups, runs October 21 to 23. Expect a wave of new results, including the full remibrutinib data.

stories.title: Could mouth bacteria explain why diet helps some people more?
stories.summary: A new Australian study will look at whether bacteria in the mouth explain why people with MS respond differently to healthy eating and exercise. It is just starting, so there are no results yet.
stories.why: What works for one person may not match the average, which is a reason to track your own results.

stories.title: FDA gives priority review to fenebrutinib pill for two MS types
stories.summary: The FDA will review Roche's oral drug fenebrutinib for relapsing MS and primary progressive MS, with a decision expected around spring 2027. It is not approved yet.
stories.why: It shows a possible new pill option for primary progressive MS is under review.

stories.title: National MS Society launches $1 billion Campaign to End MS
stories.summary: The Society says it is starting a five-year, $1 billion fundraising campaign for MS research, care and support. This is company-style news from the Society's own press release.

stories.title: About 3.1 million people worldwide now live with MS
stories.summary: The MS International Federation updated its Atlas of MS. It estimates 3.1 million people have MS, up from about 2.8 million in 2020. The authors say better diagnosis may explain much of the rise.
stories.why: It shows how many people share this condition, and that more are being counted.

stories.title: A short thinking-skills program showed early promise
stories.summary: In a small feasibility trial of 79 people, up to six sessions of personalized rehab helped people feel better about planning and managing fatigue. Results were self-reported, so this is an early signal, not proof.
stories.why: A larger trial is now under way.

stories.title: Thinner retinas were linked to slower thinking speed in MS
stories.summary: In a small study of 70 adults, thinning of the eye's nerve cell layer went with slower information processing, apart from physical disability. The authors say larger studies are needed.
stories.why: Simple eye scans may one day help track brain changes.

stories.title: More spinal fluid bands went with more brain lesions
stories.summary: In 62 people newly diagnosed with relapsing MS, higher oligoclonal band counts were linked to lesions in more brain areas and slightly poorer verbal memory. This is a link, not proof, and the authors say it is not a standalone test.

stories.title: Myelin-protecting pill nears a progressive MS trial
stories.summary: Company news: Quantum Biopharma is preparing a Phase 2 trial of Lucid-MS, cleared by the FDA. So far it has helped mice with MS-like symptoms and passed safety checks in healthy volunteers.
stories.why: It has not yet been tested in people with MS.

stories.title: Blood marker of nerve damage only partly predicted MS progression
stories.summary: In 262 people with early MS who started interferon beta-1a, blood levels of neurofilament light chain predicted progression only until MRI results were counted. Rising levels in year two went with faster brain shrinkage later.
stories.why: It shows a blood test may help track the disease, but it is not ready to guide care on its own.

stories.title: Fatigue score and a spinal fluid protein tied to hidden MS progression
stories.summary: In a small study of 81 people with relapsing MS, a fatigue questionnaire score and a protein in spinal fluid were linked to worsening without relapses. The authors say the findings are exploratory and need to be confirmed in other groups.

stories.title: Indirect comparison suggests Briumvi may slow disability more than two rivals
stories.summary: A statistical comparison of separate trials linked Briumvi to a lower risk of disability progression than Ocrevus or Kesimpta. It was funded by a company that sells the drug, and no head-to-head trial has tested it.
stories.why: Treat it as a hint, not proof, and talk with your neurologist before drawing conclusions.

stories.title: Ear-based nerve stimulation is being tested for hand problems in MS
stories.summary: A University of Colorado trial of about 70 adults is testing mild stimulation through the ear during hand exercises. No results yet; the main goal is safety.
stories.why: Hopes come from animal and stroke research, so it is unproven in people with MS.

stories.title: Lab-grown 3D mini-brain may help test drugs that repair MS damage
stories.summary: Researchers built a rice-grain-sized model from human stem cells to study myelin damage and repair. This is lab work only, not tested in people.

stories.title: Physical activity and MS risk: a possible link only with low sun exposure
stories.summary: In a Swedish study of about 3,000 people with MS and 5,800 without, activity alone was not clearly linked to MS risk. Among people with low sun exposure, the most active had 24% lower odds, a link, not proof.

stories.title: Parental stress may help explain low self-esteem in teens with MS
stories.summary: In a small study of 30 Israeli children and teens with MS, fatigue and slower thinking were tied to lower self-esteem, partly through parental stress. It was a single snapshot, so it cannot show cause.
stories.why: Support for families may matter as much as support for the child.

stories.title: Melatonin for MS: benefits still unclear, review finds
stories.summary: A review of 10 studies with 435 people with MS found no clear proof that melatonin supplements reduce relapses, disability or new MRI activity. High doses raised liver concerns.
stories.why: It shows melatonin is not a proven MS treatment, though it is often sold for sleep.

stories.title: Generic MS pills showed more varied biomarker results than brand names
stories.summary: A look back at 1,124 people with relapsing-remitting MS found more variable blood protein markers with generic teriflunomide, fingolimod and dimethyl fumarate. The study had no data on symptoms or scans, so what it means for patients is unclear.

stories.title: 15 years of safety reports on MS drugs reviewed
stories.summary: Researchers studied about 500,000 U.S. adverse event reports for MS disease-modifying drugs and found different drugs tied to different side effect patterns, such as PML with natalizumab and infections with anti-CD20 drugs. The authors say reports like these cannot show how common a side effect is or which drug is safer.
stories.why: It is not a reason to change treatment; talk with your neurologist about any concerns.

stories.title: Stem cell transplant may calm lingering inflammation in MS, small study suggests
stories.summary: In 30 adults with MS who had a stem cell transplant, some MRI markers of long-lasting inflammation (called rim lesions) faded and no new ones appeared. The study was small, had no comparison group, and the authors say larger studies are needed.
stories.why: It hints at how doctors might one day tell who benefits most from a transplant.

stories.title: Ocrevus matched fingolimod on relapses in children with MS, with fewer new lesions
stories.summary: In a phase 3 trial of 187 children and teens with relapsing MS, Ocrevus worked about as well as fingolimod for relapses and led to fewer new brain lesions on MRI. Infusion reactions were common, mostly mild or moderate. The trial was run by the drug's maker, Roche.
stories.why: Children with MS have had few treatment studies, so more data helps families and doctors choose.

stories.title: Pain linked to feeling foggy, but not to test scores
stories.summary: In 396 adults at one Canadian MS clinic, more pain went with more self-reported thinking and memory trouble. Their actual test results did not match how they felt.
stories.why: It suggests pain, mood and fatigue may affect how thinking feels, and are worth mentioning to a care team.

stories.title: Vitamin D receptor gene variants tied to MS symptoms in Greek study
stories.summary: In 200 people with MS and 265 without, no single gene variant differed by MS status. Some variants were linked to motor symptoms and neck spinal cord lesions, a link, not proof.

stories.title: Christina Applegate says doctors now doubt her MS diagnosis
stories.summary: The actor said on her podcast that a doctor told her she does not have MS and that the cause of her symptoms is unknown. Neurologists say MS can be misdiagnosed because no single test confirms it.
stories.why: It is a reminder that MS diagnosis relies on criteria, and a specialist can review a diagnosis that does not fit.

stories.title: Early CAR-T results in 3 people with progressive MS
stories.summary: At a major MS meeting, researchers reported a donor-cell CAR-T therapy called CTA313 in just three people with progressive MS. After 3 months, two improved slightly and one stayed stable; side effects were mild.
stories.why: Very small and early, so it shows only that this idea is being tested safely.

stories.title: Podcast: why dizziness and vertigo happen in MS
stories.summary: A physiotherapist explains how the body's balance system works, why MS can cause dizziness, vertigo and balance trouble, and what treatment and support exist.

stories.title: Experimental pill fenebrutinib lowered markers of chronic brain inflammation
stories.summary: Company-reported trial data say fenebrutinib cut slowly expanding lesions by up to 30% and relapses by 55% versus Aubagio in relapsing MS. The trials are still ongoing and the drug is not yet approved.
stories.why: If approved, it could add a new oral option; the FDA decision is expected in early 2027.

stories.title: One death reported in CAR-T trial for MS as early results look promising
stories.summary: Bristol Myers Squibb reported one patient died of septic pneumonia 44 days after a CAR-T infusion. Early data in 66 people (safety was the main goal) also showed promising signs in some with progressive MS.
stories.why: CAR-T for MS is still experimental and carries real risks, such as serious immune reactions.

stories.title: Progressive MS pill vidofludimus: disability trends held in open-label extension
stories.summary: In an extension of a phase 2 trial, disability trends from the main trial were kept up by people who stayed on the drug, with no new safety concerns. There was no placebo group, and the main trial missed its brain-volume goal.
